title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the word behind the word

questions.prompt: A newspaper has one line and no room for verbs, so it rebuilds this sentence out of nouns: "The government has provided free meals, and fewer children are now denied a place at school." Which headline is made of nouns that exist?

options.text: FREE MEALS PROVIDMENT ENDS THE DENIAL OF SCHOOL PLACES
FREE MEALS PROVISION ENDS THE DENIAL OF SCHOOL PLACES
FREE MEALS PROVIDATION ENDS THE DENIATION OF PLACES
FREE MEALS PROVISION ENDS THE DENYAL OF SCHOOL PLACES

questions.explanation: Turning verbs into nouns is what a headline lives on, and it is also where the ending has to be right. English keeps a Latin form for the first verb, one that changes the body of the word and not merely its tail; and it builds the second on a short ending, after turning the final y into an i, the way it does in burial and in trial. Neither ending is deducible: hanging -ment or -ation on a verb because they are frequent produces words that no dictionary has ever held, and a wrong tail is as visible to an examiner as a wrong spelling.

questions.prompt: Your Noun spidergram may hold only nouns built on a verb of this lesson. Tick EVERY word that belongs on one of its branches.

options.text: provision
expectant
denial
reduction
reduce
provided

questions.explanation: Provision, denial and reduction are the nouns of provide, deny and reduce. Two of them take -ion and one takes -al, which is exactly the point of the diagram: the family is learnt one member at a time, tail included. The three others all belong to the same lesson, and none of them belongs on the noun branch. Expectant is an adjective: it sits on the adjective branch of that very same family and describes somebody who is waiting for something. Reduce is a verb in its bare form, and provided is a verb wearing a past ending, which is still a verb.

questions.prompt: A head teacher writes to a university about a pupil: "Leila is far too careful to hand in anything she has not checked twice." What is the head teacher saying?

options.text: she is so careful that she never finishes her work on time
she has handed in work that she had not checked properly
she spends so long checking her work that it always arrives late
she is so careful that unchecked work never leaves her desk

questions.explanation: Nothing in this structure says that a quality is excessive in the sense of being a fault. It says that the quality has ruled an action out — and when the action ruled out is one nobody wants, the sentence turns into praise, and into a guarantee for whoever is reading the letter. The reflex to break is the one that hears a complaint in the little word every time, and so invents a slowness the letter never mentions. Note as well that this is a habit, not an incident: a reference describes what the pupil always does, not what she did once.

questions.prompt: A donor asks how a plate of food at midday can change a child's marks at the end of the year. Which answer sets the chain out in the order in which it really works?

options.text: the meal raises the marks first, and better marks then bring the child to school
the meal feeds the whole family, and a family that eats can pay the school fees
the meal brings the child in every day, and a child in class every day learns more
the meal makes the lessons shorter, and shorter lessons leave more time for revision

questions.explanation: An appeal that works never asks its reader to believe a miracle: it lays out links, and each one has to hold the next. Food is a reason to walk through the gate; being in the room is what puts a child in front of the lesson; and a year of lessons heard is a year of lessons learnt. Watch out for the chain that has been laid out backwards, with the result standing in front of its own cause — marks have never yet fetched a child from home. The two remaining answers invent machinery no such page has ever claimed.

questions.prompt: In the opposites game your partner answers "soft". In which of these sentences is soft the opposite of the word hard?

options.text: The wooden bench in the corridor is very hard.
The last question on the paper was hard.
She works hard on the days she has no lessons.
It is hard to believe that the term is over.

questions.explanation: An opposite answers a meaning, never a word, and this is where a memorised list turns against you. The pair you learnt holds perfectly wherever the word means difficult — a question, a piece of work, a fact you struggle to accept — and in all those sentences the answer you owe your partner is the other one. Only where the word describes what a thing is made of does your partner's answer become the right one. And in one sentence here the word is not even an adjective: it is an adverb telling you how she works, and it takes neither member of the pair.

questions.prompt: A head teacher answers a journalist: "No child in this town is denied a place at our school." What is she claiming?

options.text: she refuses to admit that some children have no place
the school will not take a child from outside the town
some children in the town refuse the place they are offered
every child in the town who asks for a place is given one

questions.explanation: Two things have to be read at once here. The verb is used in its first sense, refusing to give something to somebody; and the sentence is passive, so the children are on the receiving end and the school is the one that would be doing the refusing. Put the negative in front of all that and what is left is a promise: nobody is turned away. The verb's second sense, saying that something is untrue, would make the sentence a defence against an accusation, which is not what she has said; and it is certainly not the children who are refusing anything. As for children living elsewhere, that sentence says nothing whatever about them.
